source_text:
Ἐκ τῶν ἀποστόλων τοῦ σωτῆρος
τῶν οʹ γεγόνασιν, ὡς ἱστορεῖ Κλήμης ἐν πέμπτῃ τῶν ὑποτυπόσεων, Βαρνάβας, 128
Σωσθένης, Κηφᾶς ὁμώνυμος Πέτρῳ, Ματθίας ὁ συγκαταριθμηθεὶς τοῖς ἕνδεκα,
Εὔβουλος, Πούδης, Κρίσκης, ἐν τῇ βʹ, Βαρσαβᾶς καὶ Λίνος, οὗ μέμνηται Παῦλος
Τιμοθέῳ γράφων, Θαδδαῖος, Κλεόπας καὶ οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ.
Ταῦτα εἰσὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν προχειρισθέντων διακόνων. αʹ. Στέφανος ὁ
πρωτομάρτυς. βʹ. Φίλιππος. γʹ. Πρόχωρος. δʹ. Νικάνωρ. εʹ. Τίμων. ʹ. Παρμενᾶς. ζʹ. καὶ
Νικόλαος. Τῶν δὲ οʹ οἱ πρόκριτοί εἰσιν οὗτοι; Παῦλος, Μάρκος, Λουκᾶς, Τίτος,
Κανδάκης ὁ εὐνοῦχος, Ἰωάννης βαπτιστής.
∆εῖ γινώσκειν τὸ πῶς συνεγράφησαν τὰ δʹ εὐαγγέλια. Ὅτι μετὰ τὴν
ἀνάληψιν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ 129 τὸ κατὰ Ματθαῖον μετὰ ἔτη ηʹ, τὸ
κατὰ Μάρκον μετὰ ἔτη ιβʹ, τὸ κατὰ Ἰωάννην μετὰ ἔτη λʹ ἐπὶ ∆ομετιανοῦ τοῦ
βασιλέως, τὸ κατὰ Λουκᾶν μετὰ ἔτη ιεʹ. Τὸ κατὰ Ματθαῖον εὐαγγέλιον ἑβραΐδι
διαλέκτῳ γραφὲν ὑπ' αὐτοῦ ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐξεδώθη, ἑρμηνεύθη δὲ ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου.
Τὸ κατὰ Μάρκον ὑπηγορεύθη ὑπὸ Πέτρου ἐν Ῥώμῃ. Τὸ κατὰ Λουκᾶν ὑπηγορεύθη
ὑπὸ Παύλου ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ. Τὸ κατὰ Ἰωάννην ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις Τραιανοῦ ὑπηγορεύθη
ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ Κομόδου, ἐν Πάτμῳ τῇ νήσῳ ἐγράφη.
thought_title: The seventy, the seven deacons, and how the four Gospels were written
orientation: Epiphanius is listing the seventy apostles and the seven deacons, then recording the dates and circumstances of the four Gospels' composition.
pass_a_gloss: Of the apostles of the Savior, the seventy were, as Clement relates in the fifth [book] of the Outlines: Barnabas, Sosthenes, Cephas [the] same-named [as] Peter, Matthias the [one] numbered with the eleven, Eubulus, Pudens, Crescens, in the second [book], Barsabbas and Linus, whom Paul mentions writing to Timothy, Thaddaeus, Cleopas and those with him. These are the names of the deacons chosen [for service]. 1. Stephen the first martyr. 2. Philip. 3. Prochorus. 4. Nicanor. 5. Timon. 6. Parmenas. 7. and Nicholas. Of the seventy the chief ones are these: Paul, Mark, Luke, Titus, the eunuch of Candace, John [the] Baptist. It is necessary to know how the four gospels were composed. That after the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, the [gospel] according to Matthew [was written] after eight years, the [gospel] according to Mark after twelve years, the [gospel] according to John after thirty years under Domitian the king, the [gospel] according to Luke after fifteen years. The gospel according to Matthew, written in [the] Hebrew language by him in Jerusalem, was published, and it was interpreted by John. The [gospel] according to Mark was dictated by Peter in Rome. The [gospel] according to Luke was dictated by Paul in Rome. The [gospel] according to John in the times of Trajan was dictated by John himself under Commodus; on Patmos the island it was written.

choices.why: The glossary specifies 'the seventy' for this group of apostles distinct from the Twelve.
The glossary gives 'Outlines' as the title of Clement's work.
The glossary specifies 'first martyr' for Stephen, banning 'protomartyr'.
The term means those selected or preferred; 'chief ones' captures the sense of preeminence among the seventy.
The verb means to dictate for another to write down, which fits the tradition that Peter and Paul dictated the Gospels to Mark and Luke.
The source uses βασιλέως ('king') rather than 'emperor'; keeping 'king' preserves the source's terminology.

bible_refs.note: οὗ μέμνηται Παῦλος Τιμοθέῳ γράφων (whom Paul mentions writing to Timothy)

pass_b_english: Clement relates in the fifth book of the Outlines that among the seventy apostles of the Savior were Barnabas, Sosthenes, Cephas who had the same name as Peter, Matthias who was numbered with the eleven, Eubulus, Pudens, Crescens, in the second book, Barsabbas and Linus, whom Paul mentions when writing to Timothy (2 Timothy 4:21), along with Thaddaeus, Cleopas, and those with him.
These are the names of the deacons chosen for service: first, Stephen the first martyr; second, Philip; third, Prochorus; fourth, Nicanor; fifth, Timon; sixth, Parmenas; seventh, Nicholas.
The chief ones among the seventy are these: Paul, Mark, Luke, Titus, the eunuch of Candace, and John the Baptist.

It is necessary to know how the four gospels were composed. After the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Gospel according to Matthew came after eight years, the Gospel according to Mark after twelve years, the Gospel according to John after thirty years under King Domitian, and the Gospel according to Luke after fifteen years.

The Gospel according to Matthew was written by him in the Hebrew language in Jerusalem and was published, and it was interpreted by John. The Gospel according to Mark was dictated by Peter in Rome. The Gospel according to Luke was dictated by Paul in Rome. The Gospel according to John was dictated by John himself under Commodus in the times of Trajan, and written on the island of Patmos.

problems.quote: dictated by John himself in the times of Trajan, and it was written on the island of Patmos under Commodus
problems.source_quote: ὑπηγορεύθη ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ Κομόδου, ἐν Πάτμῳ τῇ νήσῳ ἐγράφη
problems.why: 'ἐπὶ Κομόδου' means 'under Commodus,' not 'in the times of Trajan'; Trajan and Commodus are swapped.
problems.fix: dictated by John himself under Commodus, and it was written on the island of Patmos in the times of Trajan
problems.ruling: Source says ὑπηγορεύθη...ἐπὶ Κομόδου (under Commodus); English wrongly says 'in times of Trajan' for Commodus.

problems.why: English reverses the rulers: 'under Commodus' modifies dictation, 'in the times of Trajan' modifies writing; Greek has Trajan for dictation, Commodus for writing.
problems.fix: The Gospel according to John was dictated by John himself in the times of Trajan, and it was written under Commodus on the island of Patmos

dictated by John himself in the times of Trajan, and it was written under Commodus: Greek 'ἐπὶ Κομόδου' means 'under Commodus'; reordered to 'under Commodus in the times of Trajan'.

last_rejected.why: Greek 'ἐν τῇ βʹ' means 'in the 2nd [book]' referring to Clement's work, not 'in the second book' as a separate clause. Actually this seems correct. Wait—context: 'Crescens, in the second book, Barsabbas and Linus'—this suggests Crescens was mentioned in book 2, not that Barsabbas and Linus were. The Greek structure groups Crescens with those in book 2. The English punctuation makes it ambiguous but not clearly wrong.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν τῇ βʹ correctly rendered 'in the second book'; punctuation ambiguity is not a translation error.

last_rejected.quote: The Gospel according to John was dictated by John himself under Commodus in the times of Trajan
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὸ κατὰ Ἰωάννην ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις Τραιανοῦ ὑπηγορεύθη ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ Κομόδου
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'in the times of Trajan' (temporal), then 'under Commodus' (reign). English reverses order but keeps both. Actually 'under Commodus in the times of Trajan' is awkward but not wrong. Wait—'ἐπὶ Κομόδου' = under Commodus, 'ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις Τραιανοῦ' = in the times of Trajan. The English has 'under Commodus in the times of Trajan'—this is reversed from Greek order but same meaning. However, historically this is contradictory (different emperors). The source presents variant traditions. The English preserves both names, so meaning is intact.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις Τραιανοῦ and ἐπὶ Κομόδου both preserved; order shift does not change meaning.

last_rejected.quote: The Gospel according to Luke was dictated by Paul in Rome
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὸ κατὰ Λουκᾶν ὑπηγορεύθη ὑπὸ Παύλου ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ
last_rejected.why: Greek 'ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ' = 'in Rome'. English 'in Rome'—correct.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ = 'in Rome'; translation is correct, no error exists.

last_rejected.why: The English adds a scripture reference '(2 Timothy 4:21)' not in the source text. This is an editorial addition not present in the Greek.
last_rejected.fix: whom Paul mentions when writing to Timothy
last_rejected.ruling: Editorial scripture reference (2 Tim 4:21) is a standard annotation, not a meaning change or mistranslation.

last_rejected.quote: Clement relates in the fifth book of the Outlines that
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς ἱστορεῖ Κλήμης ἐν πέμπτῃ τῶν ὑποτυπόσεων
last_rejected.why: The English inverts the source order: Greek puts the list first, then 'as Clement relates...' The English puts Clement's introduction first. This changes the rhetorical structure but not the fundamental claim. However, the Greek begins with the list ('Of the seventy apostles... were Barnabas...') and appends the source citation. The English makes Clement the grammatical subject. This alters the presentation significantly.
last_rejected.fix: Among the seventy apostles of the Savior were Barnabas, Sosthenes, Cephas who had the same name as Peter, Matthias who was numbered with the eleven, Eubulus, Pudens, Crescens, in the second book, Barsabbas and Linus, whom Paul mentions when writing to Timothy, along with Thaddaeus, Cleopas, and those with him, as Clement relates in the fifth book of the Outlines.
last_rejected.ruling: Reordering ὡς ἱστορεῖ Κλήμης to front position is a stylistic choice; meaning is unchanged.

last_rejected.quote: The chief ones among the seventy are these
last_rejected.source_quote: Τῶν δὲ οʹ οἱ πρόκριτοί εἰσιν οὗτοι;
last_rejected.why: Greek has a question mark: 'οἱ πρόκριτοί εἰσιν οὗτοι;' = 'are these the chief ones?' or 'the chief ones are these?' The Greek punctuation (question mark in Greek = ; ) suggests a question or at least a listing formula. The English flattens this to a declarative statement, losing the interrogative or formulaic force.
last_rejected.fix: Are these the chief ones among the seventy?
last_rejected.ruling: Greek ';' is ambiguous; εἰσιν οὗτοι can be declarative. Rendering as statement is within acceptable range.
